title: US-Iran War Enters 11th Night as Senate Blocks War Powers, Ukraine Defense Expo Hit by Russian Missile, India Tests Indigenous Long-Range SAM
subhead: The US completes its 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran while the Senate rejects a war powers resolution 49-47, leaving congressional oversight of the conflict unresolved. Meanwhile, a Russian ballistic missile kills 10 at a Ukrainian defense industry exhibition near Kyiv, and India's DRDO successfully tests the Kusha long-range air defense missile.

sections.heading: US-Iran War Escalates: 11th Night of Strikes, Hormuz Blockade Holds, Oil Surges Past $92
sections.body:
US Central Command confirmed the completion of an 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran, targeting aircraft hangars and drone storage sites across multiple provinces including Bushehr, East Azerbaijan, Hamadan, Hormozgan, Khuzestan, and Sistan and Baluchistan, according to Iran's IRNA news agency. President Trump stated the US had 'no interest in meeting' with Iranian officials and signaled that strikes could intensify, specifically threatening the area near Pickaxe Mountain, Iran's fortified underground nuclear site near its primary enrichment facility.

Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz remains unbroken despite the bombardment. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed responsibility for attacking a tanker in the strait on Tuesday, forcing the crew to abandon ship, and also claimed two additional ship attacks on Monday. US forces have redirected eight commercial vessels and disabled one to enforce a counter-blockade, CENTCOM said.

Oil prices reflect the disruption: Brent crude closed above $92/barrel on July 24, with day's range touching $87.68-$92.83, and US regular gasoline hit $4/gallon average. Over 500 US troops have been wounded in the conflict, according to a US official cited by AP — exceeding the Pentagon's official Defense Casualty Analysis System tally of 482 due to reporting lag.

Iran's Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni traveled to Pakistan to seek mediation, meeting with army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, who urged restraint. The interim deal signed in mid-June, a 14-point memorandum of understanding that was supposed to halt fighting and reopen Hormuz, has effectively collapsed — Iran withdrew from the MoU, and Trump told NewsNation he 'couldn't care less' about Iran's exit from the agreement, according to Al Jazeera and multiple outlets.

Meanwhile, Iran-backed Houthi rebels have opened a new front in the Red Sea, declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia — an escalation that threatens the kingdom's pipeline alternative to Hormuz. Six ships were reportedly forced to reroute in the Red Sea after Houthi warnings, according to the Houthi-run SABA news agency.
sections.whyItMatters: The Iran-Hormuz conflict has become a sustained high-intensity campaign with no diplomatic off-ramp in sight. Over 500 US casualties, oil above $92, and the collapse of the June interim deal all point to a war that is structurally expanding — not contracting. The Red Sea escalation adds a second chokepoint threatening global energy flows.

sections.heading: Senate Blocks Iran War Powers Resolution 49-47, NDAA Stalled
sections.body:
The US Senate voted 49-47 against advancing a war powers resolution that would have forced President Trump to withdraw US military forces from Iran within 60 days unless Congress explicitly authorized the action or declared war. The vote fell largely along party lines, with Senator Susan Collins (R-ME) crossing party lines to support it, while Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) was the sole Democrat to oppose. Notably, Senators Rand Paul (R-KY) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), who had supported similar measures previously, did not vote, Reuters reported.

The Senate vote came one day after the House passed its own version 214-208, with four Republicans — Tom Barrett (MI), Warren Davidson (OH), Thomas Massie (KY), and Brian Fitzpatrick (PA) — crossing party lines. The House also passed the $1.15T NDAA 216-212 on July 23, which includes the controversial Section 219 — the US-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative, which would permanently integrate Israeli technology into the US defense supply chain and require the Secretary of War to formalize joint work on counter-drone systems, missile defense, AI, quantum computing, and cyber warfare.

The NDAA now faces a Senate stalemate. Democrats are blocking the must-pass defense authorization over the Iran war, demanding war powers constraints. The Section 219 provision has drawn bipartisan opposition: former National Counterterrorism Center head Joe Kent called it 'a betrayal of our sovereignty,' and an amendment from Reps. Khanna and Massie to strip it garnered over 100 Democratic votes but ultimately failed.
sections.whyItMatters: The war powers vote reveals deep congressional unease with the Iran war — even within the GOP — but not enough to override a presidential authorization. The NDAA stalemate means the defense authorization bill, which funds the entire Pentagon, is now hostage to the Iran debate. Section 219's Israel integration provision, buried in the NDAA, would represent an unprecedented structural merger of US and Israeli defense technology chains.

sections.heading: Russian Missile Kills 10 at Ukrainian Defense Industry Exhibition Near Kyiv
sections.body:
A Russian ballistic missile struck the site of a defense industry exhibition hosted by a drone manufacturers' association near Kyiv on July 24, killing 10 people and injuring nearly 100, according to Ukraine's Emergency Services. The event was held at a private training ground in the Kyiv region, where representatives of Ukraine's defense industry were present.

The strike came just hours after President Zelensky met with Raytheon executives to discuss building Patriot missile systems in Ukraine, following Trump's approval for the arrangement. Zelensky criticized the event's organizers, stating it was 'absolutely unacceptable to hold any weapons exhibitions with large crowds of people, especially near residential buildings' under wartime conditions. Ukraine's prosecutor general opened a criminal case into possible failure of officials to ensure security.

The Ukrainian Council of Defence Industry confirmed representatives were at the site but said it had not organized the event. Valerii Borovyk, founder of drone company First Contact, confirmed the missile struck a training ground where a defense industry exhibition was being held.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia would continue fighting until 'total victory,' acknowledging that Trump's peace overtures were sincere but claiming they had been 'rejected by Ukraine, who were being incited by the Europeans.'
sections.whyItMatters: The strike highlights the operational security risks of defense industry gatherings in an active war zone — and the speed with which Russian intelligence can act on targeting information. The Zelensky-Raytheon meeting on Patriot production in Ukraine, greenlit by Trump, represents a significant shift in defense industrial policy: moving Patriot missile manufacturing closer to the front lines. Russia's response was to strike the exhibition site the same day.

sections.heading: India Successfully Tests Kusha Long-Range Air Defense Missile
sections.body:
India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) conducted the maiden flight test of the Kusha Long-Range Surface-to-Air Missile (LRSAM) from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island off the Odisha coast on July 23. The missile successfully intercepted an electronic target simulating a high-speed, high-altitude aerial threat, according to the Ministry of Defence.

Project Kusha, formally sanctioned by the Cabinet Committee on Security in May 2022 with an allocation of Rs 21,700 crore (approximately $2.6 billion), aims to deploy five squadrons for the Indian Air Force. It uses three distinct interceptor variants: the M1 (120-150 km range) against tactical aircraft and cruise missiles, the M2 (250 km range) against standoff jammers and bombers, and the M3 (350-400 km range) against AEW&C platforms and ballistic or hypersonic threats at high altitude.

The system uses dual-pulse solid-propellant rocket motors achieving speeds exceeding Mach 5.5, with a guidance suite combining inertial navigation, satellite mid-course datalink, and a dual-mode AESA millimeter-wave RF seeker with electro-optical/infrared terminal seeker. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh called the test 'a major milestone' that 'eliminates foreign import dependency for such critical strategic systems.'

The Kusha is designed to complement India's existing S-400 and MR-SAM systems, forming a layered air defense architecture. Once development and user trials are completed, the system is expected to be inducted into the Indian Air Force as part of India's broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat self-reliance initiative.
sections.whyItMatters: India joins a very small group of nations with indigenous long-range air defense capability. The Kusha program, at $2.6 billion for five squadrons, represents a deliberate shift away from import dependence for strategic air defense — directly complementing the Russian S-400s and filling the gap between medium-range MR-SAM and the longest-range S-400 engagement envelopes. If development stays on track, it also positions India as a potential future exporter in a segment currently dominated by the US (Patriot), Russia (S-400), and China (HQ-9).

sections.heading: EU 21st Sanctions Package Targets $120B Crypto Network, Expands Shadow Fleet Boardings
sections.body:
The European Union adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia, with the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas stating the package hits 'over a hundred banks and crypto operators, 40+ vessels in Russia's shadow fleet, and several oil refineries in Russia and Belarus.'

The centerpiece is an expansion targeting the A7 cross-border payments network and its A7A5 stablecoin, which Chainalysis estimates has processed nearly $120 billion to date and is 'purposely built for Russia's sanctions evasion,' according to CoinDesk. The EU extended a transaction ban to 14 unnamed crypto-related service platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the UAE, the Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus.

Notably, the package introduces a new instrument: a possible full third-country ban on crypto-asset services used by Russia, which would enable the EU to ban any transaction between an EU operator and any crypto provider used by Russia. Alongside digital asset measures, the EU is freezing assets and banning transactions for 94 banks and major financial institutions, and extending its transaction ban to 33 additional Russian credit and financial institutions.

The sanctions came just three days after Russia's State Duma passed legislation establishing the country's first comprehensive framework for regulating cryptocurrency, with most rules taking effect September 1.
sections.whyItMatters: The EU is now explicitly targeting the crypto-based sanctions evasion infrastructure that has sustained Russia's war economy. The new third-country crypto ban instrument is unprecedented — it would allow the EU to cut off any crypto exchange globally that facilitates Russian transactions, not just EU-based ones. The timing, three days after Russia formalized its own crypto regulation, signals a direct escalation in the financial dimension of the conflict.

sections.heading: Congress Moves to Block Korean-Built Warships for US Navy
sections.body:
Congress is moving to block the purchase of Korean-built warships for the US Navy, with the White House protesting the congressional restriction. According to USNI News, lawmakers inserted language in the defense authorization that would prevent the Navy from procuring vessels built outside the United States, effectively barring the Korean-built frigate option that had been under consideration as a response to the Navy's shipbuilding crisis.

The move comes as the US Navy confronts a deepening shipyard capacity crisis and has been exploring foreign construction partnerships — including with South Korean shipbuilders — as one potential avenue to accelerate fleet growth. The congressional block reflects protectionist pressure from domestic shipbuilding interests and concerns about relying on allied but foreign industrial capacity for warfighting vessels.

The White House has pushed back, arguing that the restriction eliminates a viable near-term option for expanding the fleet at a time when the Navy is struggling to meet its shipbuilding targets and industrial capacity is maxed out at domestic yards.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a concrete test of whether the US can practically increase naval capacity without allied industrial partnerships — or whether political protectionism will override operational urgency. The Navy's shipbuilding backlog and capacity constraints are well-documented; blocking the Korean option narrows the solution set without offering an alternative path to faster construction.

bottomLine: The US-Iran war has settled into a grinding pattern of nightly strikes and Hormuz disruption with no diplomatic resolution in sight, while Congress remains deadlocked — the Senate blocked war powers oversight and the NDAA is stalled. On the industrial side, India's successful Kusha LRSAM test marks a genuine breakthrough in indigenous air defense, and the EU's 21st sanctions package introduces an unprecedented tool to cut off global crypto services used by Russia. Ukraine's defense industry gathering was hit the same day Zelensky met Raytheon on Patriot production — a reminder that in this war, industrial policy and battlefield reality intersect in real time.
sources: AP, Reuters, USNI News, CoinDesk, Business Standard, Firstpost, Businessworld, ABC Australia, OAN, CNBC, Al Jazeera, Newsday, The Guardian, Korea Herald, Middle East Eye, Romania Insider, Yahoo Finance, Washington Post, MSN, Economic Times India
